explanation: From the universal law of gravitation (Eq. (7.5) in the NCERT excerpt) the acceleration produced by a mass M at a distance r is a = GM/r^2. Thus the acceleration at Earth's surface g = GM/R^2 and the acceleration of the Moon a_m = GM/R_m^2, where R_m ≈ 60 R. Taking the ratio g/a_m = (GM/R^2) / (GM/R_m^2) = (R_m/R)^2 = 60^2 = 3600. This agrees with the NCERT result shown (Eq. (7.4) giving a factor ≈ 3600). Option A (60) is incorrect because it uses the linear distance ratio instead of the inverse-square dependence. Option C (1/3600) is the reciprocal and therefore wrong sign of the comparison (it would represent a_m/g, not g/a_m). Option D (60^3 = 216000) is incorrect because it cubes the distance ratio rather than squaring it; the inverse-square law requires squaring the distance ratio, not cubing it.

stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping down an inclined plane (as described in the NCERT excerpt). Which one of the following best explains why the cylinder has angular momentum (i.e., a rotational component of motion) about its centre of mass at any instant during the roll?

options.A: Because in rolling different particles of the cylinder have different linear velocities at an instant, so the motion includes rotation about the centre in addition to translation.
options.B: Because the entire cylinder moves with the same velocity at each instant, it is in pure translation and therefore has no angular momentum about its centre.
options.C: Because the point of contact with the plane is instantaneously at rest, the only angular momentum is about the contact point and the angular momentum about the centre must be zero.
options.D: Because only the translation of the centre of mass contributes to the motion; rotation about the centre does not contribute to angular momentum.

explanation: Correct answer (A): The NCERT excerpt explicitly describes rolling down an incline as a combination of translation and rotation and notes that in rolling different points of the cylinder have different velocities at an instant (e.g. points P1–P4 have different arrows in Fig. 6.2). Those differing particle velocities indicate a rotational motion about the cylinder’s axis (i.e. about the centre), so the body has an angular (rotational) component in addition to translation. Why the others are wrong: (B) contradicts the excerpt: pure translational motion is defined by all particles having the same velocity, but the excerpt shows that rolling is not pure translation—particles do not have the same velocity—so the statement that there is no angular momentum is incorrect. (C) is incorrect because although the NCERT text notes the point of contact can be instantaneously at rest for rolling without slipping, that fact does not imply the angular momentum about the centre is zero; the body still has rotation even though the contact point’s linear velocity is zero. (D) is incorrect because it denies the rotational contribution: the excerpt distinguishes translation from rotation (rotation about an axis produces differing particle velocities), so rotation about the centre does contribute to the motion (and hence to the angular character) of the body. The correct reasoning follows directly from the NCERT discussion that rolling is a combination of translation and rotation and that particle velocities differ during rotation.

stem: Two containers of equal volume are maintained at the same temperature and pressure; one contains oxygen gas and the other contains helium gas (both treated as ideal). According to the kinetic theory ideas and statements in the NCERT excerpt on behaviour of gases, which of the following is necessarily true?

options.A: Both containers contain the same number of molecules.
options.B: Both containers contain the same total mass of gas.
options.C: Both gases have the same mean free path for their molecules.
options.D: Both gases must have the same viscosity.

explanation:
Correct (A): Avogadro’s hypothesis as presented in the excerpt and the relation PV = N kB T imply that equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. The NCERT text explicitly states that equal volumes of all gases at equal temperature and pressure have the same number of molecules (and gives the standard number for 22.4 L at STP).

Why B is wrong: The total mass depends on the molar (molecular) mass of the gas. The excerpt states that the mass of 22.4 litres of any gas equals its molecular weight in grams at STP, so equal volumes of different gases generally have different masses unless their molar masses are identical.

Why C is wrong: The mean free path is defined in the excerpt as the average distance a molecule travels without colliding and is of the order of thousands of angstroms for gases, but its actual value depends on molecular parameters (size, spacing and collision frequency). The NCERT passage links molecular parameters to measurable gas properties, so mean free path need not be the same for different gases under the same macroscopic conditions.

Why D is wrong: The excerpt states kinetic theory relates properties such as viscosity to molecular parameters. Viscosity therefore depends on molecular characteristics (size, mass, collision behaviour) and is not guaranteed to be identical for different gases even at the same temperature and pressure.

stem: The NCERT excerpt (pages 1–3 of Chapter 9, Mechanical Properties of Fluids) discusses pressure in fluids and the conditions for flow and equilibrium. Which one of the following statements is explicitly supported by the text in these pages?

options.A: For a liquid in equilibrium the pressure is the same at all points in a horizontal plane.
options.B: In a flowing fluid the pressure always decreases at locations where the fluid speed is larger (Bernoulli relation).
options.C: Bernoulli’s principle states that the total energy per unit volume of a fluid is the same at all points of the fluid, whether it is at rest or flowing.
options.D: Pressure in a liquid decreases with depth; the difference between pressures at two depths is given by P2 − P1 = −ρgh.

explanation: Correct answer (A): The excerpt explicitly states that “for a liquid in equilibrium the pressure is same at all points in a horizontal plane.” This is given in the discussion that if pressure were not equal different parts of a fluid would flow, so in absence of flow pressure must be same in a horizontal plane. Why the others are wrong: (B) The excerpt notes that unequal pressure would cause flow but does not state the Bernoulli relation that links pressure and speed in a flowing fluid; that specific claim is not presented on the given pages. (C) The provided pages do not present a statement that total energy per unit volume is the same at all points or mix the cases of rest and flow; this formulation is not given in the cited excerpt. (D) This contradicts equation (9.6) in the excerpt: for a fluid at rest the text derives P2 − P1 = ρgh (pressure increases with depth), so the form with a negative sign is incorrect according to the given material.

stem: Two small homogeneous solid spheres of different materials are placed separately in a fluid and subjected to the same uniform external pressure. Based on the NCERT discussion of hydraulic stress, volume strain and Hooke’s law, which of the following is correct about their fractional volume changes and bulk moduli?

options.A: The sphere made of the material with the larger bulk modulus will show the smaller fractional decrease in volume under the same pressure; bulk modulus = (applied pressure)/(volume strain).
options.B: The sphere with the larger bulk modulus will show a larger fractional decrease in volume under the same pressure, because a larger modulus means stronger restoring forces produce more compression.
options.C: For a given applied hydraulic pressure, the fractional volume change is the same for all materials and depends only on the pressure, not on the material's bulk modulus.
options.D: Bulk modulus equals the change in volume per unit pressure, so a larger bulk modulus implies a larger absolute volume change for the same applied pressure.

explanation: Correct answer (A): The NCERT text defines hydraulic stress (equal in magnitude to the applied pressure) and volume strain as ΔV/V. It also states Hooke’s law (for small deformations): stress ∝ strain, with the proportionality constant called a modulus of elasticity. Applying this to uniform compression gives bulk modulus K = (hydraulic stress)/(volume strain) = (pressure)/(ΔV/V). For the same applied pressure a larger K therefore implies a smaller ΔV/V (smaller fractional volume decrease). Why the others are wrong: (B) is incorrect because a larger modulus means the material resists deformation more (so it compresses less), not more. (C) is incorrect because the fractional volume change depends on both the applied pressure (stress) and the material’s bulk modulus (the stress–strain proportionality), not on pressure alone. (D) is incorrect because it inverts the relation: bulk modulus is pressure divided by fractional volume change, not fractional volume change per unit pressure (the latter would be the reciprocal of the bulk modulus).

pollen-pistil interaction is a dynamic process involving pollen recognition
followed by promotion or inhibition of the pollen. The knowledge gained
in this area would help the plant breeder in manipulating pollen-pistil
interaction, even in incompatible pollinations, to get desired hybrids.
You can easily study pollen germination by dusting some pollen from
flowers such as  pea, chickpea, Crotalaria, balsam and Vinca on a glass slide
containing a drop of sugar solution (about 10 per cent). After about 15–30
minutes, observe the slide under the low power lens of the microscope.  You
are likely to see pollen tubes coming out of the pollen grains.
A breeder is interested in crossing different species and often genera
to combine desirable characters to produce commercially ‘superior’
varieties. Artificial hybridisation is one of the major approaches of crop
improvement programme. In such crossing experiments it is important
to make sure that only the desired pollen grains are used for pollination
and the stigma is protected from contamination (from unwanted pollen).
This is achieved by emasculation and bagging techniques.
If the female parent bears bisexual flowers, removal of anthers from
the flower bud before the anther dehisces using a pair of forceps is
necessary. This step is referred to as emasculation. Emasculated flowers
have to be covered with a bag of suitable size, generally made up of butter
paper, to prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen. This
process is called bagging. When the stigma of bagged flower attains
receptivity, mature pollen grains collected from anthers of the male parent
are dusted on the stigma, and the flowers are rebagged, and the fruits
allowed to develop.
If the female parent produces unisexual flowers, there is no need for
emasculation. The female flower buds are bagged before the flowers open.
When the stigma becomes receptive, pollination is carried out using the
desired pollen and the flower rebagged.

Primary treatment : These treatment
steps basically involve physical removal of
particles – large and small – from the sewage
through filtration and sedimentation. These
are removed in stages; initially, floating debris
is removed by sequential filtration. Then the
grit (soil and small pebbles) are removed by
sedimentation. All solids that settle form the
primary sludge, and the supernatant forms
the effluent.  The effluent from the primary
settling tank is taken for secondary treatment.
Secondary treatment or Biological treatment : The primary
effluent is passed into large aeration tanks (Figure 8.6) where it is
constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped into it. This allows
vigorous growth of useful aerobic microbes into flocs (masses of
bacteria associated with fungal filaments to form mesh like
structures). While growing, these microbes consume the major part
of the organic matter in the effluent. This significantly reduces the
BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) of the effluent. BOD refers to
the amount of the oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic
matter in one liter of water were oxidised by bacteria. The sewage
water is treated till the BOD is reduced. The BOD test measures the
rate of uptake of oxygen by micro-organisms in a sample of water
and thus, indirectly, BOD is a measure of the organic matter present
in the water. The greater the BOD of waste water, more is its polluting
potential.
Once the BOD of sewage or waste water is reduced significantly, the
effluent is then passed into a settling tank where the bacterial ‘flocs’ are
allowed to sediment. This sediment is called activated sludge. A small
part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to
serve as the inoculum. The remaining major part of the sludge is pumped
into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters. Here, other kinds
of bacteria, which grow anaerobically, digest the bacteria and the fungi
in the sludge. During this digestion, bacteria produce a mixture of gases
such as methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide. These gases
form biogas and can be used as source of energy as it is inflammable.

An ecosystem can be visualised as a functional unit of
nature, where living organisms interact among themselves
and also with the surrounding physical environment.
Ecosystem varies greatly in size from a small pond to a
large forest or a sea. Many ecologists regard the entire
biosphere as a global ecosystem, as a composite of all
local ecosystems on Earth. Since this system is too much
big and complex to be studied at one time, it is convenient
to divide it into two basic categories, namely terrestrial
and aquatic. Forest, grassland and desert are some
examples of terrestrial ecosystems; pond, lake, wetland,
river and estuary are some examples of aquatic
ecosystems. Crop fields and an aquarium may also be
considered as man-made ecosystems.
We will first look at the structure of the ecosystem, in
order to appreciate the input (productivity), transfer of
energy (food chain/web, nutrient cycling) and the output
(degradation and energy loss). We will also look at the
relationships – cycles, chains, webs – that are created as
a result of these energy flows within the system and their
inter- relationship.

12.1 ECOSYSTEM – STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
In earlier classes, you have looked at the various components of the
environment- abiotic and biotic. You studied how the individual biotic
and abiotic factors affected each other and their surrounding. Let us look
at these components in a more integrated manner and see how the flow of
energy takes place within these components of the ecosystem.
Interaction of biotic and abiotic components result in a physical
structure that is characteristic for each type of ecosystem. Identification
and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem gives its
species composition. Vertical distribution of different species occupying
different levels is called stratification. For example, trees occupy top
vertical strata or layer of a forest, shrubs the second and herbs and grasses
occupy the bottom layers.
The components of the ecosystem are seen to function as a unit when
you consider the following aspects:
(i) Productivity;
(ii) Decomposition;
(iii) Energy flow; and
(iv) Nutrient cycling.
To understand the ethos of an aquatic ecosystem let us take a small
pond as an example. This is fairly a self-sustainable unit and rather simple
example that explain even the complex interactions that exist in an aquatic
ecosystem. A pond is a shallow water body in which all the above
mentioned four basic components of an ecosystem are well exhibited.
The abiotic component is the water with all the dissolved inorganic and
organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom of the pond.
The solar input, the cycle of temperature, day-length and other climatic
conditions regulate the rate of function of the entire pond. The autotrophic
components include the phytoplankton, some algae and the floating,
submerged and marginal plants found at the edges. The consumers are
represented by the zooplankton, the free swimming and bottom dwelling
forms. The decomposers are the fungi, bacteria and flagellates especially
abundant in the bottom of the pond. This system performs all the functions
of any ecosystem and of the biosphere as a whole, i.e., conversion of
inorganic into organic material with the help of the radiant energy of the
sun by the autotrophs; consumption of the autotrophs by heterotrophs;
decomposition and mineralisation of the dead matter to release them back
for reuse by the autotrophs, these event are repeated over and over again.
There is unidirectional movement of energy towards the higher trophic
levels and its dissipation and loss as heat to the environment.
12.2 PRODUCTIVITY
A constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem
to function and sustain. Primary production is defined as the amount of

207

biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by
plants during photosynthesis. It is expressed in terms of weight (gm–2) or
energy (kcal m–2). The rate of biomass production is called productivity.
It is expressed in terms of gm–2 yr –1 or (kcal m–2) yr–1 to compare the
productivity of different ecosystems. It can be divided into gross primary
productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP). Gross primary
productivity of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter
during photosynthesis. A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants
in respiration. Gross primary productivity minus respiration losses (R),
is the net primary productivity (NPP).
GPP – R = NPP
Net primary productivity is the available biomass for the consumption
to heterotrophs (herbiviores and decomposers). Secondary productivity
is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by
consumers.
Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting a
particular area. It also depends on a variety of environmental factors,
availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity of plants. Therefore,
it varies in different types of ecosystems. The annual net primary
productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately 170 billion tons
(dry weight) of organic matter. Of this, despite occupying about 70 per
cent of the surface, the productivity of the oceans are only 55 billion tons.
Rest of course, is on land. Discuss the main reason for the low
productivity of ocean with your teacher.
12.3 DECOMPOSITION
You may have heard of the earthworm being referred to as the farmer’s
‘friend’. This is so because they help in the breakdown of complex organic
matter as well as in loosening of the soil. Similarly,  decomposers break
down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon
dioxide, water and nutrients and the process is called decomposition.
Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark, flowers and dead remains of
animals, including fecal matter, constitute detritus, which is the raw
material for decomposition. The important steps in the process of
decomposition are fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and
mineralisation.
Detritivores (e.g., earthworm) break down detritus into smaller particles.
This process is called fragmentation. By the process of leaching, water-
soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated
as unavailable salts. Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into
simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.
It is important to note that all the above steps in decomposition  operate
simultaneously on the detritus (Figure 12.1). Humification and
mineralisation occur during decomposition in the soil. Humification leads

that is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition
at an extremely slow rate. Being colloidal in nature it serves as a reservoir
of nutrients. The humus is further degraded by some microbes and release
of inorganic nutrients occur by the process  known as mineralisation.
Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process. The rate of
decomposition is controlled by chemical composition of detritus and
climatic factors. In a particular climatic condition, decomposition rate
is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker, if detritus is
rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars. Temperature
and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors that regulate
decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes.
Warm and moist environment favour decomposition whereas low
temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition resulting in build
up of organic materials.

12.4 ENERGY FLOW
Except for the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem, sun is the only source
of energy for all ecosystems on Earth.  Of the incident solar radiation less
than 50 per cent of it is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).  We
know that plants and photosynthetic bacteria (autotrophs), fix Sun’s
radiant energy to make food from simple inorganic materials. Plants
capture only 2-10  per cent of the PAR and this small amount of energy
sustains the entire living world.  So, it is very important to know how the
solar energy captured by plants flows through different organisms of an
ecosystem. All organisms are dependent for their food on producers, either
directly or indirectly. So you find unidirectional flow of energy from the
sun to producers and then to consumers. Is this in keeping with the first
law of thermodynamics?
Further, ecosystems are not exempt from the Second Law of
thermodynamics. They need a constant supply of energy to synthesise
the molecules they require, to counteract the universal tendency toward
increasing disorderliness.
The green plant in the ecosystem are called producers. In a terrestrial
ecosystem, major producers are herbaceous and woody plants. Likewise,
producers in an aquatic ecosystem are various species like phytoplankton,
algae and higher plants.
You have read about the food chains and webs that exist in nature.
Starting from the plants (or producers) food chains or rather webs are
formed such that an animal feeds on a plant or on another animal and in
turn is food for another. The chain or web is formed because of this
interdependency. No energy that is trapped into an organism remains in
it for ever. The energy trapped by the producer, hence, is either passed on
to a consumer or the organism dies. Death of organism is the beginning
of the detritus food chain/web.
All animals depend on plants (directly or indirectly) for their food needs.
They are hence called consumers and also heterotrophs.  If they feed on
the producers, the plants, they are called primary consumers, and if the
animals eat other animals which in turn eat the plants (or their produce)
they are called secondary consumers. Likewise, you could have tertiary
consumers too.  Obviously the primary consumers will be herbivores.
Some common herbivores are insects, birds and mammals in terrestrial
ecosystem and molluscs in aquatic ecosystem.
The consumers that feed on these herbivores are carnivores, or more
correctly primary carnivores (though secondary consumers). Those

stem: Which combination of experimental observations from Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase (as described in NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5 §5.2) provides the strongest, NCERT-supported evidence that DNA is the genetic material?

options.A: Avery et al.: purified DNA from heat‑killed S bacteria alone transformed live R bacteria into S, and treatment with DNase abolished transformation while protease and RNase treatments did not; Hershey–Chase: bacteriophages grown with radioactive phosphorus had radioactive DNA (not protein), showing that DNA — not protein — is the viral material that enters and directs infection of bacteria.
options.B: Avery et al.: the protein fraction purified from heat‑killed S cells converted R to S; Hershey–Chase: bacteriophages grown with radioactive sulfur (labelling protein) transferred radioactivity into bacteria, proving protein is the genetic material.
options.C: Avery et al.: RNase treatment abolished the transforming ability of heat‑killed S extracts, indicating RNA is the hereditary substance; Hershey–Chase: both radioactive phosphorus and sulfur labels were detected equally in infected bacteria, so both DNA and protein carry genetic information.
options.D: Avery et al.: heat killed S cells lost all transforming ability unless DNA was present, implying a non‑nucleic contaminant was responsible; Hershey–Chase: labelled DNA and protein both entered bacteria but only protein determined progeny virions, so protein is the genetic material.

explanation: Why A is correct: The NCERT account states that Avery, MacLeod and McCarty purified biochemical fractions from heat‑killed S cells and found that DNA alone caused transformation of live R cells into S; protease and RNase treatments did not affect transformation while DNase inhibited it. This identifies DNA as the transforming (hereditary) substance. The NCERT also describes Hershey and Chase labelling bacteriophages with radioactive phosphorus (which labelled DNA) or radioactive sulfur (which labelled protein) to ask which viral component entered bacteria, and presents these experiments as the unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material. Together these observations — loss of transformation after DNase and the phosphorus labelling of the viral genetic material that enters bacteria — support DNA as the genetic material. Why the other options are wrong: B contradicts the NCERT text: Avery et al. found DNA, not protein, caused transformation, and Hershey–Chase did not show protein (sulfur label) to be the transmitted genetic material. C is incorrect because NCERT reports that RNase did not abolish transformation (Avery’s results implicate DNA), and it does not support the claim that both labels were equally found in bacteria. D is incorrect because it misstates Avery’s conclusion (the transforming principle was DNA, not a non‑nucleic contaminant) and contradicts the NCERT summary of Hershey–Chase, which supports DNA — not protein — as the material determining progeny virions.

options.A: Because the amino (–NH2) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups of amino acids are ionizable and can change their charged state with pH, producing different forms (e.g., neutral, zwitterion, or charged).
options.B: Because peptide bonds linking amino acids are readily broken and re‑formed at different pH values, changing the individual amino acid structures.
options.C: Because the R (side) group of every amino acid remains permanently uncharged, so only backbone groups determine overall ionization irrespective of pH.
options.D: Because only the R (side) group determines whether an amino acid is acidic or basic; the –NH2 and –COOH groups do not affect ionization with pH.

explanation: Correct (A): The NCERT text states that a particular property of amino acids is the ionizable nature of –NH2 and –COOH groups and that “in solutions of different pH, the structure of amino acids changes.” This means these backbone functional groups can exist in different charged states depending on pH (giving neutral, zwitterionic or charged forms). Incorrect (B): The passage describes amino acids and their functional groups; it does not state that peptide bonds are readily broken/reformed with normal pH changes. Peptide bonds form the polymer backbone but the explanation in the text for pH effects focuses on ionizable groups, not bond cleavage. Incorrect (C): The text explicitly classifies amino acids as acidic, basic and neutral (examples: glutamic acid, lysine, valine), so side chains (R groups) can be charged in some amino acids; they are not permanently uncharged in every amino acid. stem: One mole of KCl (molar mass 74.5 g mol–1) is dissolved in 1.00 kg of water. The observed elevation of boiling point of the solution is 0.88 K. Given that Kb for water is 0.52 K kg mol–1 (as in the NCERT discussion of boiling point elevation), what is the van't Hoff factor i for KCl in this solution?
explanation: From the NCERT text, for dilute solutions the elevation of boiling point is proportional to molality: ΔTb = Kb · m. If the solute dissociates into i particles per formula unit, the effective molal concentration of particles becomes i·m, so ΔTb(observed) = i · Kb · m. Here one mole of KCl in 1.00 kg of water gives m = 1.00 mol kg–1, Kb = 0.52 K kg mol–1 and ΔTb(observed) = 0.88 K. Thus i = ΔTb / (Kb · m) = 0.88 / (0.52 · 1.00) ≈ 1.6923 ≈ 1.69. This is answer A. Why the others are incorrect: B (2.00) would correspond to complete dissociation of KCl into two ions and would give an expected ΔTb = 2 × 0.52 K = 1.04 K (as the NCERT example shows), but the observed ΔTb is smaller (0.88 K), so i is less than 2. C (1.04) confuses the expected ΔTb for full dissociation (1.04 K) with the numerical value of i; 1.04 is a temperature change (K), not the dimensionless van't Hoff factor here. D (0.52) is the value of Kb (Kb for water) and not the van't Hoff factor; substituting that into the formula would not match the observed ΔTb. Thus only A is consistent with the NCERT relations and the given data.

stem: Which one of the following statements correctly describes an acylation reaction of a primary aliphatic amine as given in the NCERT discussion on reactions of amines?

options.A: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine with an acid chloride (or anhydride/ester) replaces a hydrogen of –NH2 by an acyl group to give an amide, and the reaction is carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine (for example, pyridine) to remove the HCl formed.
options.B: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine occurs with alkyl halides to give amides, and no base is required.
options.C: When a primary aliphatic amine reacts with a carboxylic acid at room temperature it undergoes acylation to give the corresponding amide directly.
options.D: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine with acid chlorides proceeds without formation of HCl, so addition of a stronger base like pyridine inhibits the reaction.

explanation: Option A is correct because the NCERT text states that aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution in which a hydrogen of –NH2 or >N–H is replaced by an acyl group to give amides, and that the reaction is carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine (e.g., pyridine) which removes the HCl formed and shifts the equilibrium to the right. Option B is incorrect because alkylation involves reaction with alkyl halides (not acid chlorides) and gives alkylated amines, not amides; the NCERT explicitly distinguishes alkylation (with alkyl halides) from acylation. Option C is incorrect because the NCERT notes that amines form salts with carboxylic acids at room temperature rather than directly undergoing acylation to give amides. Option D is incorrect because the NCERT explicitly states that HCl is produced during acylation and that a stronger base such as pyridine is used to remove the HCl; therefore a base does not inhibit but facilitates the reaction.

options.A: For many chemical reactions, an increase of temperature by 10°C nearly doubles the rate constant.
options.B: NCERT states that increasing temperature generally decreases the rate constant because molecular collisions become less effective.
options.C: For a first-order reaction, increasing the temperature increases the half-life of the reaction.

explanation: Correct (A): The NCERT text explicitly notes that "for a chemical reaction with rise in temperature by 10°, the rate constant is nearly doubled," and it also states that most chemical reactions are accelerated by increase in temperature. Thus option A matches the NCERT discussion. Why the others are wrong: B is incorrect because it contradicts the NCERT statement that reactions are generally accelerated on raising temperature (rate constants increase), not decrease. C is incorrect because for a first-order reaction the half-life t1/2 = ln2/k (given in the NCERT table); if temperature increases, k increases, so t1/2 decreases rather than increases. D is incorrect because the NCERT example for N2O5 decomposition gives half-lives that become shorter at higher temperature (10 days at 0°C, 5 h at 25°C and 12 min at 50°C), so the half-life does not become longer on raising temperature.

stem: Which of the following statements about classification of carbohydrates and their reducing behaviour is correct?

options.A: All disaccharides are non-reducing because the glycosidic linkage always involves the reducing (aldehydic or ketonic) groups of the monosaccharide units.
options.B: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because its glycosidic linkage connects C1 of glucose to C2 of fructose, thereby involving the reducing groups of both monosaccharides.
options.C: Maltose is a non-reducing disaccharide because its two α-D-glucose units linked by a C1–C4 bond leave no free aldehydic group.
options.D: Ketose monosaccharides are non-reducing, while aldose monosaccharides are reducing.

explanation: Correct option (B): Sucrose is non-reducing because the glycosidic bond is between C1 of α-D-glucose and C2 of β-D-fructose; this linkage involves the functional (aldehydic or ketonic) groups that would act as reducing groups, so those groups are not free and sucrose does not reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagents. Why the others are wrong: (A) is false — not all disaccharides are non-reducing; only those in which the reducing (aldehydic/ketonic) groups are involved in the glycosidic bond are non-reducing (sucrose is an example), whereas others can be reducing. (C) is false — maltose (two α-D-glucose units linked C1–C4) is a reducing sugar because a free aldehyde group can be produced at C1 of the second glucose in solution, so it does show reducing properties. (D) is false — all monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars; monosaccharides are defined as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones and are capable of reducing reagents.

stem: According to the Crystal Field Theory description given in the NCERT excerpt (Class XII, Ch.5 §5.5), which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Crystal Field Theory treats ligands as point charges (for anions) or point dipoles (for neutral molecules), and the asymmetrical negative field produced by such ligands lifts the degeneracy of the metal ion’s d orbitals causing their splitting.
options.B: Crystal Field Theory describes the metal–ligand bond as arising from covalent overlap of metal nd and ligand orbitals and therefore ignores electrostatic interactions between metal and ligand charges.
options.C: The five d orbitals of a metal ion lose their degeneracy only when the metal ion is surrounded by a perfectly spherically symmetric field of negative charges.
options.D: Valence Bond Theory distinguishes between weak and strong ligands by predicting different extents of d‑orbital splitting, while Crystal Field Theory does not address ligand strength.

explanation: Option A is correct because the NCERT text defines Crystal Field Theory as an electrostatic model: it "considers the metal–ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions" and explicitly states that "ligands are treated as point charges in case of anions or point dipoles in case of neutral molecules," and that this asymmetrical negative field from ligands "lifts the degeneracy of the d orbitals" causing splitting. Option B is wrong because it contradicts the NCERT description of CFT: CFT is explicitly presented as an electrostatic (ionic) model, not one based on covalent orbital overlap (covalent overlap is the picture used in Valence Bond or Molecular Orbital approaches). Option C is incorrect because the NCERT excerpt says degeneracy is maintained when the metal is in a spherically symmetrical negative field; it is the asymmetrical ligand field that lifts (not a spherical field). Option D is false because the NCERT passage notes as a limitation of Valence Bond Theory that it "does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands," implying VB cannot predict ligand strength effects on splitting; by contrast CFT addresses effects of the ligand field (i.e., why different ligand environments give different splitting).

get lodged in the body, they start a new tumor there. This property called

CIRCULATORY PATHWAYS
The circulatory patterns are of two types – open or closed. Open
circulatory system is present in arthropods and molluscs in which blood
pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or
body cavities called sinuses. Annelids and chordates have a closed
circulatory system in which the blood pumped by the heart is always
circulated through a closed network of blood vessels. This pattern is
considered to be more advantageous as the flow of fluid can be  more
precisely regulated.
All vertebrates possess a muscular chambered heart. Fishes have a
2-chambered heart with an atrium and a ventricle. Amphibians and the
reptiles (except crocodiles) have a 3-chambered heart with two atria and a
single ventricle, whereas crocodiles, birds and mammals possess a
4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles. In fishes the heart
pumps out deoxygenated blood which is oxygenated by the gills and
supplied to the body parts from where deoxygenated blood is returned to
the heart (single circulation). In amphibians and reptiles, the left atrium
receives oxygenated blood from the gills/lungs/skin and the right atrium
gets the deoxygenated blood from other body parts. However, they get mixed
up in the single ventricle which pumps out mixed blood (incomplete double
circulation). In birds and mammals, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
received by the left and right atria respectively passes on to the ventricles of
the same sides. The ventricles pump it out without any mixing up, i.e., two
separate circulatory pathways are present in these organisms, hence, these
animals have double circulation. Let us study the human circulatory
